speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INCREASES IN SALARIES, PAY AND ALLOWANCES OF CIVIL SERVICE, ARMED FORCES AND MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
I should like to make an announcement concerning increases in civil service salaries, the pay and allowances of the armed forces, and the pay of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The statement is as follows:
After a careful review of all relevant factors, the government has decided that it would be right and proper to authorize an increase in salaries in the civil service, and in the pay and allowances of members of the armed services and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The last general adjustment in rates of pay occurred in December of 1950.
As I have said on previous occasions, the government's policy in these matters is based
on two main principles. First, that salary and pay scales and other conditions of employment in both the civil service and the armed forces should be such as to attract and retain persons of the right type and necessary qualifications. Second, that having regard to the ancillary conditions of employment, remuneration for each class of work or employment should be generally in line with that paid for comparable work by good private employers.
Applying these principles to current conditions, the government believes that a broad series of pay and salary increases is now justified. These increases will apply to all ranks in the armed services and the R.C.M.P. (excluding the commissioner and the chiefs of staff) and to all classes of the civil service with the following exceptions:
(a)	The salaries of civil servants in the higher brackets will be reviewed on an individual basis.
(b)	Where it is clear that current civil service salary rates are already closely in line with rates being paid by good private employers, the civil service commission will consider whether and to what extent it would be proper to recommend specific increases.
(c)	Where the salaries paid in any class have been adjusted since December, 1950, a lesser increase than that applied generally will be authorized, again having regard to rates being paid by good private employers.
(d)	The proposed increases will apply only to classified employees. The rates of pay of prevailing rates employees, as is well known, are governed by the prevailing rates in similar private employment.
The amount of increase will vary from class to class in accordance with the basic principles to which I have already referred. The range of percentage increases will be from about 4 per cent to about 14 per cent. The general average effect of these increases will be to add between 8 and 9 per cent to the total salary, pay and allowances cost of both the civil service and the armed services. It is proposed that all these adjustments will date from December 1, 1951.
Full details of the new rates of pay and allowances in the armed services and the pay of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are being announced by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Minister of

Public Service-Pay Increases Justice (Mr. Garson) and I take this opportunity of tabling copies of these announcements. Complete details for all classes of civil servants are not yet ready. The civil service commission, however, has completed its recommendation for all the larger classes covering more than four-fifths of the personnel in the classified civil service, and I am tabling a copy of these recommendations which have been approved by the government. The remaining classes will be dealt with during the next few weeks and will be announced in the usual way as soon as they have been approved.
In the case of most departments, there have been sufficient savings in the salary votes to take care of the increased rates of pay for the remaining months of this fiscal year. Some departments may require small supplements to their salary votes before the end of the fiscal year. If that proves to be necessary, parliament will be asked early in the 1952 session to vote the required funds.
I now table copies of the schedules prepared by the civil service commission for the civil service and approved by the government and copies of the announcement and schedules issued by the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: RADAR SCREEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) referred to articles which appeared in the Montreal Herald of December 10, 11 and 12.
Perhaps it would be a fair summary of the articles to say that they allege that, despite orders for S400 to $500 million worth of radar equipment, it is doubtful if our radar defences will be completed in the three years planned and that this is because of red tape and delay in ordering and producing equipment.
The articles leave the impression that $400 to $500 million have been appropriated to be spent on equipment for the radar screen. I am unaware of the source of this figure but it is fair to say that it is a gross exaggeration. A more correct figure would be in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent of this amount. The equipment on order for the radar screen is of the latest type. Orders were placed as soon as the development work on this equipment had proceeded to a sufficient point to enable production to be undertaken. It will be appreciated that it takes about two years to construct a station of this kind and to make and instal the radar equipment. While delays are inevitable in this, as in every other country, in the production of new and complicated equipment of this kind, reasonably satisfactory progress is being made and some of the equipment has in fact already been installed. In the interim, we have equipment of the type in use at the end of the second world war.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, December 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce) for the second reading of Bill No. 41, to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, and to change its title to the Canada Elections Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADVANCE POLLS AND PRISONERS OF WAR VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the light of the friendly Christmas feeling evidenced this morning thus far, I feel we are lucky indeed to live in a country with the form of government we have here in Canada. Many people across the Atlantic would be very glad if they .were in the same position.
1924	HOUSE OF
Dominion Elections Act
In the elections committee this year, as in many other years, there was a spirit of friendly co-operation. That co-operation lasted while matters proceeded as the majority desired-and that is perhaps as one might expect. I might add however that for a number of years I have been trying to bring to the attention of the house an improved system of voting. Four or five years ago I had a bill prepared by the law clerk and, by coincidence, on the morning my bill was placed in my hands there appeared in Votes and Proceedings another bill along similar lines in the name of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). Because of the rush of other business before the house at the session it was not possible to deal with that bill.
On different occasions since that time I have brought to the attention of the committee on elections the fact that we should improve our system of voting, and I believe the reason for bringing about that improvement has not been disputed thus far.
Looking into the records since the time of my first election in 1935, I find that a number of members have been elected to the House of Commons without having received a majority of the votes cast in their constituencies. In 1935, I find, 103 members were elected by majority votes, and 138 by minority votes. In 1940 there were 162 majority candidates, and 79 minority candidates. Then, in 1945- and this may appear strange-only 99 members were elected by majority votes, while 142 came to the House of Commons with minority votes. In the 1949 election 142 members were elected by majorities, and 116 by minorities. The government has approximately 190 seats out of 262 and I believe they got 49 per cent of the vote polled. In my opinion that is not giving the kind of representation to which we are entitled in a good country like Canada. There should be some other method of voting which will give us the proper representation and prevent any member coming to this house unless he has received at least 51 per cent of the vote polled.
In addition to myself and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, there are other people in Canada who feel that our system should be changed. About two and a half years ago the Canadian Chamber of Commerce took up this matter and considered it worthy of some research. They requested their various branches across the dominion to indicate what they thought about having another system of voting which would bring about the results I have mentioned, that is, not allowing a member to come here without having a majority of the votes cast in his constituency in a particular election.


The chamber of commerce stated that if a sufficient number of their branches across the country were in favour of having a change made they would press the matter further. Apparently that majority was obtained because they made a request to have another method of voting adopted. When the committee met during the last session another letter was received from the secretary of the chamber of commerce reminding the committee of the request that had been made by that organization.
To carry this along a little further, we find that in the election held on November 22 in Ontario the Progressive Conservatives obtained 79 seats although they received only 49 per cent of the votes; the Liberals obtained 7 seats although they received only 31 per cent of the vote, and the C.C.F. obtained 2 seats although they received 19 per cent of the vote. Anyone who considers those figures must realize that things are not as they ought to be. When people come here to speak for their constituents they should have better backing than many have at the present time.
In my own particular constituency there were five candidates running in 1945. Had the vote been split up fairly evenly it would have been possible for a member to have been sent here after receiving only 25 per cent of the vote, or perhaps even less. In my opinion that is not good business. In the last election there was one candidate elected in Toronto who received 38J per cent of the vote. This man belongs to the communist party. We are sending thousands of our men overseas and spending millions of dollars in fighting communism, yet under our method of voting one of their spokesmen sits in the legislature at Toronto. It may be necessary for me to deal more in detail with that a little later on.
This matter was brought up in the committee on November 15 last. I did not bring in an amendment at that time, but I did bring up the question for consideration. After I had explained this somewhat the chief electoral officer was called. I must say that he is doing a good job and in doing that he is following in his father's footsteps. Since I came here in 1936 I have had the best of cooperation and service from the former chief electoral officer and the gentleman who holds that office at the present time, and I think every hon. member of this house has had similar treatment. I hope that continues.
The chief electoral officer made quite an exhaustive presentation. There were two hon. members in particular who objected to the method of voting. I might say that in

Manitoba and Alberta we have a form of alternative vote, but that does not give the results which I want to get in the dominion elections. Under that system a person may vote for only one candidate and stop right there. That is what we call plumping. The result is that many members are elected without having a majority of the votes polled.
In Australia they have compulsory registration and compulsory voting. They use a system of marking ballots which I should like to see used here. I am not at this time suggesting that we have either compulsory registration or compulsory voting. The method that I advocate is that where there are three or more candidates on the ballot the voter must mark his choice right down the line. In doing that he can give his last choice to the fellow he least desires to be elected. I think that would take care of the trouble we have at the present time. I should like to quote from the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) before the committee, as reported on page 134 of the proceedings, as follows:

According to my figures, in the general election of 1949 some 121 members were elected by minority votes cast in their ridings. I have a short article here that appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on August 24 of that year. It is a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa and reads:
A record total of 5,856,307 votes was cast in the June 27 general election compared with 5,246,130 in the 1945 election, it was disclosed Tuesday by Jules Castonguay, chief electoral officer. The Liberal party, returned to power with an overwhelming majority, received 2,926,029 votes in the last election compared with 2,170,625 in 1945. The Progressive Conservatives, second largest group in the commons, hold 1,742,235 compared with 1,455,453; the C.C.F., 790,321 against 822,661, and the Social Credit party 139,801 against 214,998.
These figures indicate that it required approximately 15,160 votes to elect a Liberal member in 1949 whereas it took approximately 42,540 votes to elect a Progressive Conservative. As has been pointed out, this situation might easily be reversed because in the recent Ontario election-and I have not seen a break-down yet-some 49 per cent of the votes cast elected 79 members to the Frost government out of a total of 90 seats. Before a candidate is declared elected I think it is very essential that he should have received a majority of the votes cast in the riding.
Those of us who have followed elections in the past know very well that there have been situations where a third and sometimes a fourth candidate has been brought into the field to split a certain vote. That has been recognized in several parts of the country, and it is only by an amendment providing for the transferable vote that you can overcome that system in an election. Where people can pretty well judge what the result will be I think it is very bad that a third or fourth candidate should be introduced simply to split the vote and change the representation of the riding. As I see it, that is not in the interests of democracy.
In the 1949 election just under 50 per cent of the vote resulted in the Liberal party obtaining 75 per cent of the seats. Thirty per cent of the vote resulted in the Progressive Conservatives obtaining 16 per cent of the seats. Thirteen per cent of the vote resulted in the C.C.F. winning 5 per cent of the seats, and 7 per cent of the vote gave the Social Credit party and others 4 per cent of the seats. That is a very unfair situation. At this late date I do not want to go into great detail. I want to repeat what the hon. member for Battle River said, namely, that

for a great many years this system has been in operation in the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba. I have read editorials in some eastern newspapers to the effect that it would make the determining of the result too complicated. I want to say that is far from the fact because if people will converse with those who have been in charge of the elections in Manitoba and Alberta they will find it is a simple matter to make these transfers and ascertain who has received a majority of the votes cast in a particular riding. I simply want to make this appeal once more. While it probably cannot be done at the present session, I ask the minister responsible and the members of the house to give serious consideration, before another general election is held, to amending the elections act in order to make provision for the transferable vote so that many things that have happened in the past will not be possible under what I think should be a democratic system of voting in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make a few remarks when the bill had gone into committee, but in view of the speeches which have been made, I think perhaps this would be a better place to express my opinion. I believe that this change, doing away with the word "dominion" in the Dominion Elections Act, is unwise for two reasons. Dominion Elections Act within one week, I think it was, of the dominion election in 1949. In 1945 the elections were also held at dates which were quite close together. It is hard enough to keep the election activities separate without having all dominion election material showing just the word "election" rather than the two words "dominion election". From a practical point of view I think it is unwise to make this change. People understand the word "dominion" as meaning the difference between dominion and provincial with regard to elections; and if there is one act in which we should keep the word "dominion" it is this election measure.
My second objection is based on the ground that hundreds of thousands of people in this country-in fact, I believe millions of people -place great value on the word "dominion" and they resent this policy of the government of making that word almost out of order, as we would say in this house. To Canadians who feel as I do about the matter, the word "dominion" implies vastness. It means that we think of Canada as a great country, extending from sea to sea and from the boundary of the United States to the northern reaches. It is something of which we are proud. It makes us think of this country as one of the great nations of the world.
I admit that in other parts of Canada the word may not have that same meaning. To us it implies in no way whatsoever subservience to any other race, any other nation or to anyone at all. It implies no subjection and no inequality with them. Such an interpretation does not enter into our thinking. We are no less proud of the word "Canada". I remember the great pride with which I wore the word "Canada" on my shoulder straps overseas, and I am sure that the feeling was held by every Canadian in the Canadian corps in the first war. No doubt it was just the same with Canadians who served in the second world war. We threw our shoulders around a bit just because the word "Canada" was on those shoulder straps. But little did I think that 35 years from that time I would be sitting in a Canadian House of Commons and hearing the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) making statements which insinuated that anyone who wanted to use the word "dominion" was not a good Canadian. That was the effect of the statements made by the Prime Minister on that occasion in this house a few weeks ago when this question was up. While I am on my feet may I make a vigorous protest against the substitution of the word "Canada" for the word "Dominion" in the Dominion Elections Act. The people are protesting. I have before me petitions from many organizations. Only a few days ago I received one signed by seventy-two members, and another one signed by fifty members of the Imperial Order, Daughters of the Empire. These people are protesting, and I do not blame them.

speechtext:
An ex-Conservative became a good Liberal. Firstly, Canada, in the British North America Act, was never mentioned by the name "Dominion of Canada". The name was "one dominion under the name of Canada". That fact was established by many in this house, by the Prime Minister, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others, that Canada is one dominion under the name "Canada." I wish we could put that into the mimdis of hon. members once and for all.
Secondly, Canada as a dominion ceased to be a dominion the day in 1931 that the Statute of Westminster provided that all the nations of the commonwealth are:
Autonomous communities within the British empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
Therefore, if Canada is a dominion, then the United Kingdom is a dominion and the United States is a dominion. On the one hand, previous to the Statute of Westminster -I wish my hon. friends of the Conservative party would take a few notes at this time- previous to the Statute of Westminster, no legislature in Canada could pass any law repugnant to the law of the United Kingdom. Under the statute, no law enacted in the future by Canada or any of its provinces shall be void on the ground that it is repugnant to the law of the United Kingdom.
On the other hand, the legislature of the United Kingdom cannot, under the Statute of Westminster, pass any act extending to Canada as part of the Canadian law unless it is expressly declared in the act that the Canadian parliament has requested and consented to the enactment.
Another provision of the Statute of Westminster states that neither Canada, nor any province thereof, shall in future be described as a colony or something that means colony in any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom.
When the expression "Dominion of Canada" is used abroad in the United Kingdom what does it mean? It means to indicate the idea of subordination of these dominions to the United Kingdom. That is what it means, although it might be that the expression is used carelessly and merely because it has been common to use it since those days when it was proper; that is, when the word "dominion" is used in our own country it indicates the acceptance of constitutional subordination, unless the excuse is careless speech. The word "dominion" as applied to Canada, or in>
Dominion Elections Act any act of the Canadian parliament, has now lost its original meaning in practice-I say this with all respect to my colleagues of the Conservative party-as the supremacy [DOT]of the United Kingdom is now denied in Canadian affairs, both domestic and external, since Canada has now become a sovereign state and enjoys full international status on the basis of an equal nation within the commonwealth under the provisions of the Statute of Westminster dated December 1931.
The use of the word "dominion" as applied to Canada gives a false impression as to the present constitutional position of our country, as it denies recognition of the autonomous status of Canada and implies the idea of subordination to another country. It is further misleading as it suggests to the popular mind in our country and to the populations of other countries of the world that Canada has a status which is less than sovereign. Therefore, the word "dominion" should be eliminated from our vocabulary.
I should like to quote briefly from Time magazine of May 10, 1948, in order to prove the statement I have just made. It will be remembered that I introduced a bill to strike out the word "dominion" from all acts and regulations, and this is what this publication had to say:
C.C.F.'ers and many a Liberal cheered. From the Tories came a chorus of "No! No!" Arsenault's private bill had little chance of passage. Snapped the Ottawa Journal:	"... A very silly notion.
Words or the lack of them do not make our independence." But many loyal pro-empire Canadians agreed with Arsenault's purpose, if not his motive: they were tired of explaining to Americans that ^'dominion" does not imply "domination."

speechtext: Is the United Kingdom a dominion?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADVANCE POLLS AND PRISONERS OF WAR VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Certainly, the United Kingdom is a dominion of His Majesty. That can be proved conclusively-if we discuss this thing impartially and intelligently instead of with prejudice-it can be proved by simple reference, among other things, to the form of the third prayer used daily in the House of Commons of Canada, which opens:
Most Gracious God, we humbly beseech Thee, as for Great Britain, Ireland, and His Majesty's other dominions, so especially for Canada-
The French version reads:
Dieu plein de graces, nous vous implorons hum-blement en faveur de la Grande-Bretagne, de l'lr-lande et des autres possessions de Sa Majeste.
It seems to me that it is demonstrated conclusively that in both languages, in the prayers we use daily in the House of Commons, the simple meaning of the word "dominion" is, a dominion of His Majesty. We refer to "Great Britain and His Majesty's other dominions", showing that we clearly understand the United Kingdom to be, in that regard, in the same position as Canada, a dominion of His Majesty.
It is in that sense that the use of the word "dominion" becomes dear to us, and full of meaning. Because we see in it not in any sense a connotation of being subject or inferior to the United Kingdom, but simply a recognition of the fact that Canada, together with the other self-governing nations of the commonwealth, is a dominion of His Majesty, and therefore we see it as a symbol of the common allegiance we all owe to the crown.
Dominion Elections Act
I cannot for the life of me see how even my good friends opposite, who have carried on this sort of discussion in the past with heat and prejudice, could find anything objectionable in that use and interpretation of the word "dominion", which is borne out by the authorities, by the prayers we use in the House of Commons, by a dictionary definition in an American dictionary-and by the facts.
In so far as this particular bill is concerned, we can see the matter in its true light when we compare the old title in the French version of the bill with that in the English version. We say that there is no need to eliminate the word "dominion", because it does not in any sense mean inferiority or subjection to another country. As used so frequently in titles of bills, it serves no other purpose than a connotation first of continuing allegiance to the crown which unites us, and second as a convenient method of distinguishing dominion, or federal, from provincial matters. In this instance we can see clearly that it has no other implications; and I cannot see why my hon. friends opposite should insist that it is desirable to eliminate the word "dominion" from the English version, because if hon. members will look at the French version-the version in the other official language of the house-they will see that section 1, which we are now discussing, and which gives the present title of the act, reads as follows:
L'article premier de la loi des elections fede-rales,...
That is the French name of the bill.
Loi des elections federales
So that in this case the English word is translated by the word "federales"? Do my hon. friends find anything obnoxious in the word "federales"? Is not Canada a confederation? Why do my hon. friends insist so vehemently that the word "Dominion" should be eliminated from the act? In their own version it has nothing more than the connotation of federal as opposed to provincial. Why do they not accept our assurance that, to us, it means nothing more than first, a recognition of that allegiance to the crown which unites us, and which we all owe, and that when used in this connotation or in this type of legislation it has, in addition to that, only the meaning and connotation of "federal" as distinguished from "provincial"? It has no other meaning.

I ask them to realize that it would be as logical for them to complain of the use of the word "Canada" as having colonial implications as it is for them to complain of the use of the word "dominion" as having colonial implications.
That implication and complaint I reject absolutely, in both cases. But I do point out that, if we are to consider this matter impartially and fairly, it must be kept in mind that "Canada" was the name of two of the provinces of this country when they actually were colonies, and were not self-governing, and that the word "dominion" did not come into use in connection with this country, as part of our name, until we had graduated from that colonial status, through the British North America Act of 1867, into the status of a self-governing nation, which was then called "the Dominion of Canada."
So if we are going to be logical about this matter we would have to admit that there is more reason, in logic, to attach a colonial


implication to the word "Canada" than there is to attach a colonial implication to the word "dominion". But there is no reason, in fact, sentiment or logic, to attach a colonial implication to either word.
Therefore I say that the two words should be carried forward together as descriptive of our status, of the grandeur of our land, of our affection for His Majesty and as expressing our loyalty to the crown which unites us, and will in the future as it has in the past, as one "Dominion of Canada."

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say only a word. I am not going to deal further with the definition of the word "dominion" which I think has been dealt with adequately already. But I do wish to deal briefly with one point. I do wish to make this point clear, that there is not a single person in this party that anyone in this house can honestly suggest has one iota of the feeling of subservience to any country outside our own-not a shred of it.
My purpose is to show that, so far as our party is concerned, the whole history of the party makes it clear beyond peradventure, not to be guessed at, but to be taken by the action of those who are leaders of the party.
The hon. member for Three Rivers has already spoken of 1867, and the leaders of those days, Macdonald and Cartier. I come to the next great step, the greatest step in the establishment of our independence and our position as a sovereign state which I think any fair-minded man will agree took place in 1918 and 1919 when Sir Robert Borden- and it was not an easy task-insisted that we sign the treaty of Versailles in our own right.
I admit that until then there was a good deal of the feeling of colonialism toward us in Great Britain-and for all I know there may have been some here. But the first step was when Sir Robert Borden was placed in a position where he was able to say, "We sign this treaty on our own, as a sovereign state". That is what was done. No one can suggest that any other attitude has ever existed so far as this party is concerned. Let us take the next step. The next important step, and certainly very important, was when Mr. Meighen was prime minister and went to London where he resisted the attitude of the British government in the imperial conference of 1921. He was responsible for something that no doubt was of great

importance. He was responsible for the nonrenewal of the Anglo-Japanese agreement. Does that sound like subservience to the United Kingdom? Nothing of the sort. He took his position as the representative of a sovereign state.
It may be said-and I will come to it- that there were still some technical legalities which had to be cleared up and they were cleared up later. I will come to that in a minute. Borden and Meighen took that stand, and later on there was the Statute of Westminster. I do not take one iota of credit from the people who carried that through, Mr. King and the others; of course not. But that was in the main a tidying-up operation, a continuation of what had already been done. We need not dispute about that. Let us agree that both took part in it. I am not anxious to derogate from what Mr. King did.
Let me give you one other thing. How did our party win the election of 1930? It was on the cry, "Canada first". Some people may have forgotten that. I suppose it had been thought before that that perhaps Mr. Bennett was something of an imperialist and that he was going to defer to the United Kingdom and put us in a subordinate position. Does anyone suggest that Mr. Bennett put us in a subordinate position in 1932? Hon. members will recall perfectly well what happened then. If there was any subordination it was not on the part of Canada. It was the other people who were here. Those are the points I want to make, and whatever else is said I hope that as decent honest men trying to help this nation we will not misrepresent each other's feelings, and that merely because there are different definitions of the word "dominion" in the dictionaries no one will suggest that anyone on this side of the house has one trace in his makeup of a desire that this country should be anything other than what it is, an autonomous nation. As a matter of fact, as has been well pointed out, autonomy was won by French-Canadian, English-Canadian and other Canadian soldiers on the battlefields in the main, and I hope that nothing will be done here to disturb the unity that was their creation.

Here we find the members of the House of Commons discussing the elimination of this word "Dominion", and some of them seem desirous that it be eliminated from the background of Canadian history. All this is occurring at a time when there is a war in Korea, and when we may shortly be engaged in a life and death battle. It strikes me that there are a few members in the house who seem to feel that they must


take from Canadians something that is very dear to them because some person might think we are inferior. Some Canadians cherish their historical background, and it makes for better Canadians. I am sick and tired of hearing people referred to as English or French Canadians. I hear hon. members of the house ask questions concerning how many French Canadians are fighting here, or how many French Canadians are in the civil service. We should stop that and refer to Canadians as Canadians.
I speak from a background of ancestors who have lived in this country for 150 years. The only people I know in the British isles, Germany, France or India are the people I have met as a young man going about in this country. I am a Canadian. There were French people from that marvellous province of Quebec who proved that they were Canadians by fighting side by side with me. Tiheir forefathers fought on the St. Lawrence river with my greatgrandfather. They were Canadians. The fathers of confederation fought back and forth verbally and established the great Dominion of Canada. These history-making men, these nationmaking men, these far-sighted men decided to give this country a name which would serve to let the generations to come know that colonial Canada had been welded into an everlasting nation. They gave it the name of the Dominion of Canada. Some people would like to set aside the historical facts concerning how this Canada of ours was made a nation and created the Dominion of Canada. There seems to be a concerted attack on all the historical connections between this country and France as well as those between this country and Great Britain. Why? Will any man in this house stand on his feet and say that we have ever suffered because of any connections with Great Britain or the people of France? We grow strong by trials and tribulations. No matter what our forefathers may have done, I am sure that they did those things because they believed they were right. Out of their efforts, and through their trials, this nation known as Canada has been created. It is the envy of the world today because of the calibre of the people who are really Canadians.
What a man who has been elected to the House of Commons sees in trying to break down the historical foundations of Canada, which he knows a great number of people love, I do not understand. Perhaps people believe they can be elected by crying about something that is meaningless. Take away the word "dominion" because these people believe it is historically necessary, take away the little things they cherish, and what will we have? There are some people in this

country who would like to say the King of England is not the King of Canada. I go on record as saying he is the King of Canada. If we lose that connection with empire, we have lost what Germany is seeking today, a figurehead that everyone can respect; something for which France would be a better nation. Spain would be a greater nation if she had a common tie such as the one which binds the people of this country, and binds the people of the empire together. The people of the United States know that they would be a better nation if all the people could come together under a common symbol as we do.
I was in the United States, in the city of Philadelphia, when King George V was dying. Many of the people of that city came to me with their expressions of sympathy, and you would have thought that he was their king. There were announcements of sympathy on the radio, and the newspapers had a black border of mourning. In the great Wanamaker's department store every window on the main street displayed the sympathy of the people for the people of England, as a demonstration of the reverence in which the people of the United States held our king. The great trouble with France today, with its many parties in power, is that the people have nothing to bind them together. It will be a sorry day for Canada when we cannot live in unity with the other great nations of this empire. When our dearly beloved Princess visited this country, surely hon. members must have listened to the radio and heard the cheers that accompanied her along her route. These cheers accompanied our beloved Princess from coast to coast.
I plead with the government to give up their persistence or we shall have party politics. One half of the country will cheer one man and the other half will cheer another. There will be no binding power. I say, stop in your tracks, stop in your efforts, or you are headed for that. I say this as a Canadian. I am sick and tired of politicians trying to destroy something the other man loves, be its origin British, French, German or any other. If a Canadian likes it, if he feels he needs it and it is not going to hurt us materially, let us be big enough not to take away what he believes is dear to him and what we believe is dear to us. Stop this racial prejudice that exists in Canada amongst Canadians. Stop this trying to incite your constituents to point their finger from one end of Canada to the other or halfway across. Stop these references to French Canadians and English Canadians. Refer to Canadians. Bear

I do not think that the experience in other countries has been to the effect that compulsory voting has worked out well. Indeed if at this time a citizen has to be forced to exercise the basic right upon which freedom is based, there is something wrong with his conception of citizenship.
I thought I should like to point out one thing. On one occasion during the course of a meeting in my constituency, a question was raised with regard to compulsory voting. Among those present was an elderly gentleman who made his contribution. He said that over the years he had given consideration to means of assuring the preservation of democracy which, as he pointed out, could only be preserved through the general and intelligent use of the franchise. This gentleman said that he had read that in Australia and in New Zealand-particularly in Australia-the compulsory vote was used and that it had not worked out well, even though it had assured that some 91 per cent or 92 per cent of the people cast their votes. He said that he had given consideration to an alternative-and I pass it on to you, Mr. Chairman-which would do away with the necessity of compulsory voting but would assure that people would indeed exercise their franchise. This old homesteader's plan

Dominion Elections Act was that no one should have the right to go on the voters' list unless he registered and, at the same time, paid a fee of $2. At the time he came to vote, a part of the ballot would consist of a counterfoil which would entitle the person who had voted to the return of the $2. Except when he or she is also a member of the -active service forces of the Canadian forces, a member of the regular forces, may,-[DOT]

Mr. Speaker, without entering into the controversy which developed in the discussion which took place before, may I say that I have before me now the authority for which I was looking earlier, and I should like to read it into the record for the information of hon. members. It is a letter reporting to the Queen's secretary on discussions with the Canadian delegates regarding confederation. A moment ago I

indicated the exact reference at page 394, where it is found under the heading, "The Earl of Carnarvon to General Grey":
Dear General Grey,-The North American delegates are anxious that the United Provinces should be designated as the "Dominion of Canada."
I should point out that this is dated at the colonial office, February 7,	1867, and I
should add that the words "Dominion of Canada" are in quotation marks, with the word "dominion" italicized. It continues:
It is a new title; but intended on their part as a tribute to the monarchical principle which they earnestly desire to uphold. I see no objection to the proposal. It will give greater dignity to the commencement of this great scheme and consequently greater self-respect to those who take part in the administration of affairs there. I have spoken to Lord Derby on the subject. But it remains to ascertain whether, assuming the Queen to approve of the name of Canada, Her Majesty also approves of this proposed designation of the territory. May I ask ycu to take the Queen's pleasure upon this point and to let me know?
The point which emerges clearly, which we have been discussing, for which we have been contending, and which I repeat, is that in the use of the word "dominion" there is not the slightest connotation of subjection or subordination. It is now and always has been to us, and was intended at the inception of our nation, by those who first proposed the use of the term, as a tribute to the monarchical principle which they earnestly desired to uphold. And for the same reason and in the same spirit, in an earnest desire to uphold the monarchical principle in Canada, as loyal and affectionate subjects of His Majesty, we desire to retain that word "dominion".
Motion agreed to, bill read the third time and passed.

National Gallery
hard to see that justice is done to other departments of life. Nevertheless I feel that we must try to escape that danger. I am sure we will all agree that a national art gallery is one of the things which should be regarded as .a public responsibility. The Massey report has this to say on page 77:
The national art gallery has been in temporary quarters for seventy years. It was founded in 1880 by the Marquess of Lome, who selected the pictures which were then lodged with the Department of Public Works.
And later on.
The gallery's collection of Canadian art is the most complete in existence, and the European collections, although not fully representative, are regarded as important by well-informed authorities in Canada and from abroad.
And then I quote from page 79 as follows:
The national gallery states that it can only with difficulty carry on even its present services unless certain immediate needs are met.
I direct those words to the attention of hon. members. The report continues:

The second pressing need, according to the brief, is a new building.

Also without

Mr. Chairman, when

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PROVIDE FOR TWO ADDITIONAL COMMISSIONERS, ETC.
speechtext:
When the parliamentary
assistant introduced this bill he called it a simple bill. If this bill is simple, then the bill covering the St. Lawrence seaway authority, as well as several other bills that have been considered by this house, are also simple. The parliamentary assistant has told us that the annual expenditure of this North Fraser harbour commission amounts to between $50,000 and $60,000 a year. Yet there is a section in this bill asking that the commission be increased: to five members. This week the same department brought to this house the bill covering the St. Lawrence seaway authority. If I read that bill correctly the authority would consist of a president and two other members. So we are faced with the situation where the St. Lawrence seaway authority, which will be spending hundreds of millions of dollars per year, is composed of three members, yet we are asking this house to consider a bill that will increase the North Fraser harbour commission to five members, which body spends approximately $60,000 a year. We also agree that the national harbours board, with their tremendous responsibility in Canada, can get along very well at the present time with two members. Yet the North Fraser harbour commission must have five. The New Westminster harbour commission, which is directly east of the North Fraser, will have this year something like 400 ocean-going vessels under its control; yet over the years they have done very well with three members. For some reason unknown to me, however, someone wants to put five members on this commission.
To some extent I want to go into the matter of my interest in this bill; because it is most important that, when I oppose a bill presented by a minister of this government

North Fraser Harbour Commission whom I greatly respect, I should have definite and proper reasons for doing so. About two-thirds of the shore line of the north arm of the Fraser is also the shore line of the municipalities of Burnaby and Richmond which I have the honour to represent in this house. The other third, approximately, belongs to the city of Vancouver. The city of Vancouver and the two councils of Burnaby and Richmond have bitterly opposed the passing of the first section of this bill, and that is why I am speaking at this time. When my people are against something and it is fitting, according to my judgment, that I should speak against it, then I am at all times going to accept the opportunity of speaking against it, even though a minister of the government proposes it.
As it happens, the Richmond Times-a paper put out in the municipality of Richmond-in an editorial some months ago pointed out that the commission was changed about June, 1950. Up to that time, when the old commission sat there seemed to be not too much trouble in regard to whether there should be additional members of the commission. But for various reasons that I do not intend to go into now it was considered by the Department of Transport that this commission should be changed; and it was changed, and will give better administration to the north arm of the Fraser. At that time, before the change, I can tell the committee now it was not possible to take an audit of the books. In fact it was most difficult to get the auditors to express an opinion at all on the commission. When I was elected in June, 1949, this matter was brought to my attention and I, properly I think, brought it to the attention of the Minister of Transport. He immediately took action on it and two members of the commission were changed. Since that time a senior officer of the Department of Transport has visited the commission and I have a copy of the letter he has written to the commission praising them highly for the efficient work they are now doing.
This is the first time, I think-and I do not believe the parliamentary assistant will contradict this-that the commission for the north arm of the Fraser river has ever shown a reasonable operating profit. The reason they are showing an operating profit now is that every industry on the north arm is having to pay its share, whereas in bygone days -and not too far bygone-some people were paying their share and some were not. I think it is the industries that were not paying their toll which are putting up the fight for the two additional members on the commission.

The committee will remember that this bill was brought to the house at the last session. It has been told to me-and I have represented it to the proper authorities-that it was because of a certain meeting in Vancouver not long ago, in connection with the visit of the Minister of Transport to Vancouver, that representations were made by industry that they should be represented on the commission. It is because of that meeting, I think, that this bill is presented to the committee now.
I take exception to the first section of the bill; I take no exception to the second section. The reason I take exception to the first section is this. I told the committee quite clearly that there are authorities administering many hundreds of millions of dollars which are considered by the government able to operate quite effectively with a small number of commissioners. Yet I must consent, being a member of this committee, to a small part of the national life of Canada, the north arm of the Fraser, having five members on that commission-not I think by any wish of the Minister of Transport but because it is the wish of the industries on the river who wanit control of the North Fraser board1.
It will have to be proved by the parliamentary assistant before this committee finishes its deliberations-because I intend to get to my feet again-that the present commission is inefficient. I think I can prove in this committee that it is one of the outstanding federal bodies in British Columbia. If the parliamentary assistant wishes to argue that point I am prepared to prove that it is efficient.
Before I finish with what I am going to say -and I shall not be long because I seldom take too much of the time of this chamber-I want to go into the personnel of the commission as it is at present constituted. Mr. Tom Brooke, who has been an official on this part of the river for sixteen or seventeen years, in my opinion is an able administrator. I think his heart and- soul are in the business of the commission. There are times when I do not agree with him; nevertheless he has done a good job on the north arm. I think it is a good appointment of the Department of Transport and I support Mr. Brooke in what he has done. Mr. William Lees, who lives in the municipality of Burnaby, is a recognized property evaluator in that part of the country, a man who is most necessary to the commission because of the foreshore rights that are being rented, leased and sold over the years. Mr. R. M. Grauer for twenty years was the reeve of the municipality of Richmond which is greatly interested in this bill. I do not think

the parliamentary assistant or anyone else will say that any one of those three men has shown inefficiency in regard to his operations on the commission.
I say the commission is efficient, and I will take that view until the parliamentary assistant is able to prove me wrong. Then what is the reason for changing the commission? Does it not seem rather laughable to most of the members of this committee- when I tell you, as I have, that these other great authorities on waterways across the country can operate with two and three men -that a sixteen-mile stretch of water, that for the most part is not much more than half a mile wide at its widest part and a little less than that at its narrowest part before it gets to New Westminster, has to have five members?
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that something more than common sense is behind this bill. The people of Burnaby-Richmond, in the words of the reeves,-and the parliamentary assistant has those wires as well as I-bitterly oppose this section of the bill. The original North Fraser Harbour Commissioners Act properly sets out that the interests of the municipalities are to be studied and protected as best that can be done by the federal government. In this case we are not protecting the municipalities. The city of Vancouver has also opposed this section of the bill.
There are 400,000 people or more represented by those three councils. Is this committee to study the interests of the 400,000 people, or is it to study the pressure that has been put on certain people by a few industries on the north arm of the Fraser who are interested only in their bank balances and their financial balances at the end of the year?
I said I intended to speak on this again before we finished it in the committee, but I do formally and on the record oppose the amendments to the North Fraser Harbour Commissioners Act as bitterly as I can, knowing that I am supported by every council on the lower mainland of British Columbia, and knowing that it is a wrong thing for this committee to impose upon my people two more members of the commission for which there is no need. Mr. Chairman, if this commission is inefficient this is not the way to make it efficient. If we have members on the commission who are not doing their job I would be the first in this house to rise in my place and recommend to the Minister of Transport that they be asked to resign, and we would replace them by men who could do the job. But I am convinced that this is a proper commission and that it can do
North Fraser Harbour Commission a good job, and I am waiting very anxiously and with some interest to hear the parliamentary assistant prove me wrong.

This is a rather unusual attitude for the parliamentary assistant to take. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has made out a very good prima facie case, and I think he is entitled to a reply from the parliamentary assistant. However, I should like to say a few words on section 1 and to suggest to the parliamentary assistant that he drop it.
No one is quarrelling with section 2 of the bill. Section 1 merely increases the number of harbour commissioners from three to five, and in addition-and this is a very important addition-it provides that four of these commissioners must be appointed by the government. The present set-up is that there are three commissioners, of whom one is appointed by the three municipalities of Vancouver, Burnaby and Richmond. The other two are appointed by the government. If this section is passed the municipalities will still have only one member on the commission and the government appointees will number four instead of two.
It is very significant that these three municipal organizations have all opposed section 1. When the North Fraser harbour commission was established in 1913 it was provided that the profits made by the operations of the commission would belong to the municipalities. Incidentally, in 1913 Vancouver was not involved but there were two municipalities called South Vancouver and Point Grey which have since become part of the city of Vancouver. The three municipalities are the bodies that are interested in any profits made from the operations. Therefore the operations of this commission are of prime importance to them.
Furthermore there must be some neutral control of this harbour commission, and I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that the municipalities are the proper people to have such control. They are not subject to influence by different groups in the same way that other appointees would be. If there is any body in a position to appoint commissioners whose sole interest is the protection of the public, that body is these municipalities.

Well, you hear a lot from your side of the house, so you should. We have here public bodies who are responsible to the people of the district and who in addition will gain from the proper administration of this seaway. As I have intimated, they are unanimous in opposing this section. They do not want to have the number of commissioners increased from three to five. If the government is not satisfied with the present commissioners, then it is its responsibility to change them. That is not what is being done. Those two men, who presumably do not meet with the favour of the government, are being left on the commission, and two other men are to be added. On the face of it that shows there is something not right with this proposal.
Another fact which is of great importance is that it would be unfair and unwise to place the control of this waterway in the hands of the people who have foreshore rights to acquire, who may want to get rights to ereot docks and piers, who may want rights for booming grounds. There are millions of feet of saw logs stored in the North Fraser and there are very valuable rights to be acquired by the lumber people and other industries that use the waterway or that have operations on the North Fraser. I do not believe it is sound to turn over control of the waterway to representatives of the people who are doing their business on the waterway, and who stand to profit from being able to get benefits which might not come to them
fMr. Green.]

if it were under the control of the municipalities, or of an impartial body, or of a power which had absolutely no interests at stake.
It should be a cardinal principle in setting up these commissions that power ought not to be given to the people who are going to be doing business with them. Control should be kept in independent hands, and today that is the position. This commission is under the control of independent people. Someone does not like it and wants to have a change made. Representations were made a year ago showing that there is an attempt to get at least a strong voice in the operations of the commission. For many years we had a harbour board in Vancouver, the best harbour in Canada, and one which does a tremendous business. We had only three commissioners for that harbour, and they were not appointed on the recommendation of the people who were doing business with the harbour board.
I believe the same plan should be followed in connection with the North Fraser harbour commission. In reality I think this is a Liberal party matter. This trouble arises, and the bill becomes a necessity, because of trouble in the Liberal party. I have here a dispatch from the Vancouver News-Herald, reporting an interview with the Minister of Fisheries upon his return recently from Japan. The article states:
Mr. Mayhew says he favours the three-man harbour commission if a certain one of the present three members will resign, and if Mr. Goode will live up to his promise to obtain that resignation.

Surely there is no one in this house, no matter how naive he may be-I am not suggesting that members are naive-who cannot see something fishy in connection with the North Fraser harbour board.
I have in my hand a copy of the Richmond-Marpole Times, a weekly paper published in the area served by the North Fraser harbour board. The editorial in this issue is very much opposed to what is being attempted here, that is to increase the board from three to five members. It points out, as has been pointed out already by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Bumaby-Richmond, that the municipalities concerned not only are not asking for this but are definitely opposed to it. The editorial reads:
The industrial forces behind the move to change the North Fraser harbour commission from three members to five have claimed that such reorganization is necessary in the interests of efficiency.
It indicates the organizations which are behind the move to increase the membership of the board as follows:
B.C. Lumber Manufacturers' Association
B.C. Towboat Owners Association
Salmon Canners Operating Committee

The editorial goes on to point out that the new commission is certainly not inefficient when the present revenues are compared with those obtained under the old commission. The total revenue for 18 months under the old commission amounted to $37,938.72 as compared with $84,001.89 for 16 months under the new commission. It would appear that there could not be inefficiency there. If an attempt is made to force this through the house we shall have to oppose it because a case cannot be made out for appointing five commissioners to handle a revenue of $50,000 or $100,000 a year. There is no reason in the world why that should be done except to serve the interests of people who want to get control of the board. We might as well be straight on that and act accordingly. I suggest to the government that they withdraw the bill and not perpetrate this sort of thing on the people of the North Fraser river.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PROVIDE FOR TWO ADDITIONAL COMMISSIONERS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not intend to delay the house long in rising to speak in support of the bill. I should like to point out, however, that while a three-man commission is probably satisfactory as a harbour board lor Vancouver, and probably three men are sufficient on the larger project on the St. Lawrence river, I do not think a three-man commission would be satisfactory at the present time in this situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PROVIDE FOR TWO ADDITIONAL COMMISSIONERS, ETC.
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PROVIDE FOR TWO ADDITIONAL COMMISSIONERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I will tell you why. In the first place the government has recognized two of the municipalities in the past. All three men on the board at the present time live in either Burnaby or Richmond. Vancouver's representative, while living in another municipality, has large holdings adjacent to the bridge. That does not mean to say I think that man would not be satisfactory, but the principle of giving representation to municipalities that do not contribute anything toward the support of the waterway has been recognized. Any revenue derived is divided with the municipalities. Some of the revenue goes to the provincial government, but all expenditures on the north arm of the Fraser come from the funds of the federal government. I think the very fact that there would be five men on the commission would make the situation more secure. If you want to change the present membership of the board representatives of the lumber industry, the fishing industry or any other industry could be appointed. There would be nothing to hinder the appointment of representatives of the lumber, fishing or tugboat industries, and they would have complete control of it.
With a five-man commission, and four of them appointed by the federal government, there is very little chance of any one industry or person imposing his will on the other four people on the commission. That is one reason I am supporting the bill. At one time I thought three members would be sufficient, but with only three members on the board there was no way to provide representation for all the municipalities affected. It might have been preferable to do what is being done with respect to the St. Lawrence waterways. The different municipalities and cities along the St. Lawrence river are not being brought into the picture and asked to take a part. The dominion government is going to appoint engineers who will be able to deal with the size, depth and width of the canal and how it is going to be operated. Nobody else is going to be allowed to have any say about it because they are not paying for it.
If we were to do the same thing here it might be the best way; but these same municipalities would be the very ones to object to taking that kind of stand. Therefore in order to protect the Fraser river from becoming the preserve of any special group on the river we are far better to have five commissioners rather than three, particularly when those three come from outside the area where most of the money is being
Foreign Exchange Control spent. After all, the revenue of the commission comes from money paid by people who-live along the river. It is not from the municipalities. It is revenue collected from the' people along the river. Therefore I think they have the right to some say, but they have no right to dominate the commission and impose their preferences. Rather than there being something fishy about the matter, it would be far more liable to be fishy with'-only three men on the commission rather than five. I support the bill because I think it is the right thing to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXEMPTION OF ALL CLASSES OF TRANSACTIONS FROM PERMIT REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Foreign Exchange Control welcome developments have naturally caused me, as the responsible minister, to give earnest consideration to the question whether the time was approaching when I could recommend to the government that exchange control be done away with. In considering this question, it has fortunately not been necessary for me to make any forecasts regarding the tranquillity or roughness of the waters which lie ahead; my task has been the more limited one of trying to decide whether there is sufficient likelihood that we shall wish to make use of foreign exchange restrictions to deal with whatever problems do in fact arise in the future to justify the continued retention of the powers contained in the Foreign Exchange Control Act and the administrative apparatus necessary to carry out its provisions.
The conclusion I have come to is that we would be better advised not to rely on exchange restrictions, but rather on the general handling of our domestic economic situation to keep us in reasonable balance With the outside world and to maintain the Canadian dollar over the years at an appropriate relationship with foreign currencies. This view has been shared by my colleagues, and the government has today amended the foreign exchange control regulations so as to exempt all classes of transaction covered therein from permit requirements. I shall lay on the table of the house a copy of the order in council by which this has been done. Its general effect is that foreign exchange control has been abolished in Canada.
It is the present intention of the government to introduce at the next session of parliament if the legislative program permits, and at all events before the present act expires, a measure repealing the Foreign Exchange Control Act and substituting therefor a new exchange fund act drafted along the same general lines as those parts of the Foreign Exchange Control Act which have to do with the operation of the exchange fund. Meanwhile the exchange fund, which holds the official reserves of gold and foreign currencies, continues in being and in operation under the Foreign Exchange Control Act and is available to contribute to orderly conditions and as a factor of stability in the exchange market.
Foreign exchange control was one of the basic, instruments for effective utilization of our resources for the conduct of the war. During that period and during the period of post-war readjustment the circumstances and problems which arose often placed a heavy burden upon the administrative staff. On this


occasion I wish to express, on behalf of the government, appreciation of the efficient and devoted services which the staff has always given in the fulfilment of its duties. I wish also to express appreciation of the co-operation we received from the agents of the board, business organizations and the public generally. I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to table these orders.

I thought the Minister of Fisheries had effectively answered the criticism of this bill. There are several features, however, particularly those which refer to the department upon which I think I should properly give the house some explanation. The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested that something more than the usual procedural delays accounted for the fact that this bill had not come before the committee earlier. I want to assure him that had nothing to do with the wishes of our department. At the beginning of this session this particular bill, as well as another harbour bill, were assigned to me by the Minister of Transport as those which he hoped I would guide through the house. It is recognized by all hon. members that the minister has had probably as great a responsibility in piloting legislation through this house as anyone on the front bench. It was always considered that this bill had less importance when compared with other items on the order paper. On the other hand it was realized that, since it was coming close to Christmas and the interest in the bill was chiefly on the part of members from the far west, the measure should be proceeded with even though there are other items on the order paper of greater importance. I have been here night after night waiting for this item to be called, and ready to go ahead if the procedure permitted.
Something has been said about the size of this commission. There are a number of harbour commissions composed of three people, but there are others that have five. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond said that I should establish the inefficiency of the present commission. Well, Mr. Chairman, that is the farthest thing from my thought. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that if the government has not confidence in its two nominees on this commission, it has the responsibility to replace them. The government has the authority to replace them, but that is not the issue. I do not for a moment propose to establish any lack of confidence in the men. While I agree with hon. members who have said that three of the municipalities concerned have urged that the commission be not increased, two of those municipalities have been persuaded through attending a joint meeting of the users of the harbour that there was some lack of confidence in the case of one municipality in two commisioners, and in the case of another municipality in one commissioner.
The Minister of Fisheries has suggested that by broadening this board it will rest better with all those who are users of this harbour. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond asked if there were any harbour
North Fraser Harbour Commission commissions that had direct representation of industry. I do not think there is any intention of giving any particular industry, as such, the right to nominate a direct representative on this commission. On the other hand, the board of trade in the city of Toronto nominates one of the five members of that harbour commission. I am sure that, just like any member of this house, any person who has had business experience and who is placed on this commission will feel that he is a public servant. He would disregard his personal interests, and I am sure that would be the case even if the commissioner happened to have experience in the various industries that were the chief users of this harbour.
There was a suggestion that in comparing the revenues for the present year with those of 1949 one could make some assessment of the work of the present commission. I say that statement is neither to be challenged nor defended. It is a matter of fact that in the intervening year harbour rates were substantially increased, so that is not a yardstick that could guide the house. I might point out also that in the neighbouring harbour of New Westminster the government has the authority to appoint all the commissioners. It is established by what the Minister of Fisheries has said that additional investments in this harbour were made, not by the municipalities concerned but by the federal government. I might just put the figures on record which indicate that in the last fiscal year the federal government, in addition to the moneys expended by the harbour commission, spent $298,000 on this harbour for wharf construction and dredging. In the previous year the federal investment in this harbour, quite apart from the expenditure of the commission, was $358,696. We do feel that two more commissioners should be appointed since the city of Vancouver, one of the largest municipalities concerned, has not actually a representative on this commission. That might come about through this amendment.
